cards.q: What does it mean for a system to be scalable?
cards.a: It can handle more users, data and requests just by adding resources, without being rebuilt. Test: if traffic doubles, can I just add machines, or must I change the design?

cards.q: How is scalability different from speed?
cards.a: A system can be fast for 100 users and fall over at 10,000. That system is fast, but not scalable.

cards.q: What are the three shapes of growth, and what does each one hurt first?
cards.a: More **requests** hit the app servers and the database. More **data** hits database disk and makes queries slow. More **users far away** feel latency.

cards.q: What is vertical scaling, and why is it attractive?
cards.a: **Scaling up**: making one machine stronger with more CPU, more memory (RAM) or a faster disk. It is very simple: no code changes, and all data stays in one place.

cards.q: What are the downsides of vertical scaling?
cards.a: There is a ceiling (the biggest machine you can buy), you pay for the peak all day, it is a single point of failure, and an upgrade often needs a restart.

cards.q: What is horizontal scaling?
cards.a: **Scaling out**: adding more machines and spreading the work across them. A load balancer sits in front and sends each request to one of them.

cards.q: What are the good sides of horizontal scaling?
cards.a: Almost no ceiling, it survives a machine dying, it uses many cheap normal machines, and the cloud can auto-scale: add machines when traffic goes up, remove them when it goes down.

cards.q: What makes horizontal scaling harder than vertical scaling?
cards.a: More moving parts to watch, servers must not keep user data in their own memory (they must be **stateless**), and spreading one database across many machines is hard.

cards.q: In practice, how do you combine vertical and horizontal scaling?
cards.a: Scale the app servers **out**, and scale the database **up** as far as it sensibly goes before you split it.

cards.q: What is the usual order of steps as a system grows?
cards.a: One server → database on its own machine → more app servers behind a load balancer → cache and read replicas → queues, then shard → CDN and more regions.

cards.q: Which part is almost always the hardest to scale, and why?
cards.a: The **database**. It becomes the **bottleneck**: the slowest part, which limits everything else. App servers are easy to copy. Data is not.

cards.q: How did Stack Overflow handle its traffic for many years?
cards.a: It scaled up: a small number of its own servers, with a few very powerful SQL Server database machines. Big machines plus good caching went a very long way.

cards.q: What is the difference between availability and reliability?
cards.a: **Availability**: is the system up when I need it? **Reliability**: does it work correctly, every time, over a long period? An ATM that is on but sometimes gives the wrong cash is available, not reliable.

cards.q: How much downtime per year do 99.9%, 99.99% and 99.999% uptime allow?
cards.a: Each extra nine means 10 times less downtime. 99.9%: about 8.8 hours (say 9). 99.99%: about 53 minutes. 99.999%: about 5.3 minutes.

cards.q: Why does five nines need automatic recovery?
cards.a: It allows only about 5 minutes down per year. A person doesn't even have time to notice the problem and log in.

cards.q: What happens to availability when parts are in a chain?
cards.a: It goes down, because all parts must work, so you multiply. A load balancer, app server and database at 99.9% each give about 99.7%.

cards.q: What happens to availability when two servers run side by side?
cards.a: It goes up, because the system is down only if both are down. Two servers at 99.9% are both down 0.001 × 0.001 of the time, so the pair is up 99.9999%.

cards.q: When does a second server side by side fail to raise availability?
cards.a: When the two don't fail **independently**. Two servers on the same power supply can die together.

cards.q: What is a single point of failure, and how do you find one?
cards.a: Any one part that takes the whole system down when it breaks. Point at each box and ask, "What happens if this one dies?" If everything stops, it is a SPOF.

cards.q: What are common single points of failure?
cards.a: One database with no copy, one load balancer, one data center or cloud region, one DNS provider, and hidden ones: one config server, one shared cache, or one person who knows how to deploy.

cards.q: What techniques make a system more available?
cards.a: Redundancy (spare copies), failover (switch to the spare automatically), health checks, replication, many zones, graceful degradation and careful deploys.

cards.q: What is an availability zone, and what is a region?
cards.a: A **zone** is one or more data centers with their own power and network, separate from the others. A **region** is an area, like Mumbai or Virginia, with several zones close to each other.

cards.q: Why run in several zones, but not always in several regions?
cards.a: Two or more zones is the normal setup. Several regions protect you from a whole region going down, but cost much more.

cards.q: How should you choose an availability target?
cards.a: Pick the target the product really needs, because each extra nine costs a lot more money and work. A payment system needs more nines than a company's internal lunch menu.

cards.q: What caused the AWS S3 outage in February 2017?
cards.a: An engineer ran a command to remove a few servers, but one input was typed wrong, so far more were removed. S3 in the US East region was down for about four hours.

cards.q: What is Netflix's Chaos Monkey?
cards.a: A tool that randomly shuts down servers in production during working hours. Every team must build services that survive a lost server, because it happens all the time.

cards.q: Using a 30-day month, how much downtime per month do 99.9%, 99.99% and 99.999% allow?
cards.a: 99.9%: about 43 minutes. 99.99%: about 4.3 minutes. 99.999%: about 26 seconds. Each extra nine cuts it by 10 times.

cards.q: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
cards.a: **Latency** is how long one request takes. **Throughput** is how many requests the system can finish every second.

cards.q: Where does the latency of one request come from?
cards.a: The network (distance to the server), waiting in line when the server is busy (queueing), and doing the work: running code and reading from the database or disk.

cards.q: How can you lower latency?
cards.a: Put data closer to users (CDN, more regions), cache popular data in memory, make fewer round trips, speed up queries with indexes, and do slow work later with a queue.

cards.q: What do QPS, RPS and TPS mean?
cards.a: Queries, requests and transactions per second. They all mean roughly the same thing: how many requests per second. For video or file downloads, throughput is data per second (**bandwidth**).

cards.q: Why should you design for the peak, not the average?
cards.a: Traffic is not flat: people use apps more in the evening, during a sale or during a big match. The peak is often 2 to 3 times the average, and much more during special events.

cards.q: Why can the average latency hide a problem?
cards.a: If 980 of 1,000 requests take 50 ms and 20 take 3 seconds, the average is 109 ms, which looks fine. But p99 is 3,000 ms: 2 users in every 100 wait 3 seconds. So use p50 and p99.

cards.q: Why do the slowest requests (the tail) matter so much?
cards.a: The slow users are often your best users: the biggest carts, the most friends. And one page often needs many calls, so with fan-out, rare slowness on each server becomes common slowness for users.

cards.q: What is Little's Law?
cards.a: **requests in progress = throughput × latency**. If a server can work on only 100 requests at once, 0.1 s each, it finishes 1,000 per second; at 0.2 s each, only 500. If traffic stays the same instead, slower requests mean more requests in progress.

cards.q: How does a server's busyness affect latency?
cards.a: Under about 50% busy: little waiting. About 70 to 80%: some waiting, and latency starts to rise. Over 90%: long lines, latency shoots up and timeouts start. So add servers before 100%.

cards.q: How do batching, caching and queues affect latency and throughput?
cards.a: **Batching** raises throughput but adds latency, like a bus that waits until it is full. **Caching** improves both. **Queues** give the user a fast answer and do the slow work later.

cards.q: How should you write latency and throughput in your non-functional requirements?
cards.a: With numbers and percentiles, and plan for the peak. For example: "Opening a short link should take under 100 ms at p99. About 12,000 reads per second on average, so design for around 30,000."

cards.q: A request waits for 100 servers, and each is slow 1 time in 100. How often is the user's request slow?
cards.a: All 100 are fast only 0.99 to the power 100 ≈ 37% of the time, so about **63%** of user requests are slow. Rare slowness on each server becomes common slowness for users.

cards.q: What are arrival rate, service time and utilization?
cards.a: **Arrival rate:** how many requests come in per second. **Service time:** how long one takes to handle, not counting the wait. **Utilization:** how busy the server is = arrival rate ÷ service rate. 80 per second at 10 ms each = 80%.

cards.q: In the simple M/M/1 model, what is the average wait in the queue?
cards.a: **utilization ÷ (1 − utilization) × service time.** 50% busy → about 1× the service time, 80% → 4×, 90% → 9×, 99% → 99×. It is a simplified model, but real systems show the same shape: flat, then a steep wall near 100%.

cards.q: Why does waiting explode as a server gets close to 100% busy?
cards.a: Requests arrive in random bunches, and the server needs free time to clear each line. At 50% busy it has plenty. At 99% it has almost none, so every small bunch leaves a line that takes a very long time to clear.

cards.q: An API gets 1,000 requests per second, and each takes 0.2 s. How many are in flight?
cards.a: Little's Law: 1,000 × 0.2 = **200 requests in flight** (started, not finished). With one thread per request, you need at least 200 threads across all servers, and more for the peak.

cards.q: What happens to requests in flight when a dependency gets slow?
cards.a: They grow, even with the same traffic. At 1,000 per second, going from 0.2 s to 1 s per request means 1,000 in flight instead of 200. Threads and connection pools run out, and one slow database can freeze many app servers.

cards.q: How can Little's Law size a database connection pool?
cards.a: 2,000 requests per second × 10 ms holding a connection = **20** connections in use on average. If the database slows to 50 ms, you need **100**. If the pools only have 50 in total, requests wait in line for a connection.

cards.q: When is it fine to run a server near 100% busy?
cards.a: For background or batch work, where nobody waits for each item: throughput matters, not latency. Latency-sensitive servers need headroom (a common rule of thumb: around 50 to 70% busy at peak), because waiting explodes near 100%.

cards.q: How do queues cause tail latency?
cards.a: Unlucky requests arrive just after a burst and wait behind it. In the M/M/1 model, p99 is about 4.6× the average: at 80% busy with 10 ms of work, the average is 50 ms, but p99 is about 230 ms.

cards.q: What practical rules keep queues from hurting latency?
cards.a: Leave headroom. Give every queue a size limit. Use timeouts, and drop requests that already waited longer than the caller will wait. When full, shed load (fast 503s) or push back on the sender. Watch queue length and wait time.

cards.q: What risk does Amazon's article "Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs" warn about?
cards.a: During an outage, messages keep arriving but aren't processed, so a big backlog builds. After the fix, it must all be worked through, so the service stays slow long after the cause is fixed. Measure the age of messages, not only the count.

cards.q: M/M/1 model: a server does 10 ms of work per request and is 90% busy. How long does a request wait, and how long in total?
cards.a: Wait = 0.9 ÷ 0.1 × 10 ms = **90 ms** in the queue. Total = 90 + 10 = **100 ms**, 10 times the work itself. At 50% busy it would be 10 ms of waiting and 20 ms in total.

cards.q: What is "state" on a server?
cards.a: Anything a server remembers between two requests: who is logged in, what is in the shopping cart, how much of a file has been uploaded.

cards.q: What is the difference between a stateful and a stateless server?
cards.a: A **stateful** server keeps the knowledge in its own memory, so only it can serve that user. A **stateless** server keeps nothing between requests: the request carries it, or it is read from a shared store.

cards.q: What goes wrong when app servers keep sessions in their own memory?
cards.a: The load balancer can't pick freely, a crash logs users out and loses their carts, scaling down and deploying are hard, and load can be uneven.

cards.q: Why do stateless servers scale easily?
cards.a: Any server can handle any request. Adding a server is easy, a crash loses nothing, and deploys just replace servers one at a time.

cards.q: Where should state live instead of in the app servers?
cards.a: Sessions in Redis or a signed token (JWT), carts in Redis or the database, users and orders in the database, files in object storage like S3, and waiting work in a queue.

cards.q: Why is Redis fine for sessions but not for orders?
cards.a: Redis holds state you can afford to lose now and then: if sessions are lost, users just log in again. Data that must never be lost goes in the database, which keeps copies and backups.

cards.q: Which parts of a system must be stateful?
cards.a: Databases and caches, live connections like WebSockets, multiplayer game servers, and live document editing.

cards.q: How do you handle the parts that must be stateful?
cards.a: Keep them few and separate, keep a map of who is where (like "user 42 → chat server 7" in Redis), route by key, and save state often so a new server can take over.

cards.q: What are sticky sessions?
cards.a: A load balancer setting (also called **session affinity**) that sends all of one user's requests to the same server, usually by setting a cookie.

cards.q: What are the downsides of sticky sessions?
cards.a: Uneven load, users still lose their sessions if the server dies, and it is harder to remove servers and deploy.

cards.q: When are sticky sessions okay to use?
cards.a: As a temporary fix for an old app that keeps sessions in memory, or for live connections, where the server really must stay the same. For normal web apps, move the state out.

cards.q: What does The Twelve-Factor App say about state?
cards.a: App processes should be stateless and share nothing. Anything that must be kept goes into a backing service, like a database, and sticky sessions should never be relied on.

cards.q: How does Kubernetes run stateless apps vs stateful apps?
cards.a: Stateless apps run as a **Deployment**: every copy is the same and can be replaced at any time. Stateful apps run as a **StatefulSet**: each copy gets a fixed name and its own disk.

cards.q: What is a load balancer?
cards.a: It sits in front of a group of servers and decides which server gets each request. Users see one address; behind it there can be 2 servers or 2,000.

cards.q: What are the main jobs of a load balancer?
cards.a: Spread the load, skip dead servers, give one address for many servers, and extras like TLS termination (decrypting HTTPS once, so the servers don't have to) and routing by URL.

cards.q: How does round robin work, and what is its weak spot?
cards.a: It sends requests in turn: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3. It ignores how busy each server is, so one server can get stuck with several slow requests while another sits idle.

cards.q: When would you use weighted round robin?
cards.a: When servers are different sizes. Give a 16-CPU server weight 2 and an 8-CPU server weight 1, and the big one gets 2 of every 3 requests.

cards.q: How does least connections work, and when is it better than round robin?
cards.a: It sends each new request to the server with the fewest open requests right now. It is better when requests take very different times, and for long-lived connections like WebSockets.

cards.q: When would a load balancer pick the server by hashing a key?
cards.a: When the same user or key must reach the same server, because that server keeps something for it: a cache, a chat room, a game match. Use consistent hashing, so adding a server moves only a few keys.

cards.q: What is the "power of two choices" algorithm?
cards.a: Pick two servers at random and send the request to the less busy one. It is good for very big systems with many load balancers.

cards.q: What is the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer?
cards.a: **L4** sees only IP addresses and ports, so it is very fast. **L7** reads the whole HTTP request (URL, headers, cookies), so it can route by path, host name, header or cookie.

cards.q: When would you use an L4 vs an L7 load balancer?
cards.a: L4 for huge traffic and non-HTTP traffic, like games and databases. L7 for most web apps and APIs. Big systems often use both: a fast L4 layer at the edge and L7 behind it.

cards.q: What does it mean to drain a server?
cards.a: Before removing a server on purpose, like during a deploy, the load balancer stops sending it new requests but lets requests in progress finish. AWS calls this the deregistration delay.

cards.q: How do you stop the load balancer from being a single point of failure?
cards.a: Never run just one. Use an active-passive pair with a floating IP, an active-active pair, or a managed cloud load balancer, which already runs on many machines across zones.

cards.q: How does an active-passive load balancer pair work?
cards.a: Both share one virtual IP. The active one takes all traffic. The passive one watches its heartbeat and, if heartbeats stop, takes over the address within seconds. A common tool is keepalived.

cards.q: What must each load balancer in an active-active pair be able to do?
cards.a: Carry the full load alone. Both take traffic, but if one dies, the other takes everything.

cards.q: What are Google Maglev and Facebook Katran?
cards.a: L4 load balancers that run as software on ordinary servers instead of special hardware. Maglev uses its own form of consistent hashing; Katran uses XDP and eBPF to handle packets very early.

cards.q: How does a typical health check work?
cards.a: The load balancer calls an address like `GET /health` every few seconds. A `200 OK` answer means healthy. An error, or no answer in time, means not.

cards.q: What are the four main settings of a health check?
cards.a: Interval (how often, e.g. every 10 s), timeout (how long to wait, e.g. 5 s), unhealthy threshold (failures in a row before removal, e.g. 3) and healthy threshold (passes in a row before it is added back, e.g. 2).

cards.q: Why not remove a server after one failed health check?
cards.a: Networks have small hiccups. Servers would keep dropping out and coming back. This is called **flapping**.

cards.q: What is the difference between a shallow and a deep health check?
cards.a: **Shallow**: is the program running, and can it answer? **Deep**: can it really do its job? It also tests the database connection, the cache and free disk space.

cards.q: What should the health check that decides traffic test, and why?
cards.a: Only what the server itself owns. If it tests the shared database and the database gets slow, every server fails at once, all are removed, and the whole site goes down.

cards.q: What is the difference between active and passive health checks?
cards.a: **Active**: the load balancer sends test requests. **Passive**: it watches real traffic and takes out servers with many `5xx` errors or timeouts. Envoy calls this **outlier detection**.

cards.q: How do health checks let a system heal itself?
cards.a: A failing server stops getting traffic, the auto-scaler starts a new one, and once the new one passes its health checks, the load balancer sends it traffic. No human is needed at 3 a.m.

cards.q: What is service discovery, and why is it needed?
cards.a: Finding a service's current addresses by its **name**. Servers come and go and their IPs change, so an IP like `10.0.3.17` written in a config file breaks when that server is replaced.

cards.q: What is a service registry, and how does it stay up to date?
cards.a: A live list of services and the addresses of their healthy servers. Servers register when they start, stay on it through health checks or heartbeats, and are removed when those fail or stop.

cards.q: What is the difference between client-side and server-side discovery?
cards.a: **Client-side**: the caller asks the registry and picks a server itself (Netflix Eureka). **Server-side**: the caller sends to one fixed address, like a load balancer, which looks up the registry (Kubernetes Services).

cards.q: What are the tradeoffs of client-side vs server-side discovery?
cards.a: Client-side needs a discovery library in the caller, but has no extra hop. Server-side needs nothing special in the caller, but adds a network hop through the load balancer.

cards.q: What is the weak spot of using DNS for service discovery?
cards.a: DNS answers are cached for their TTL, so a dead server's address can be returned for a while.

cards.q: What is the difference between a liveness and a readiness probe in Kubernetes?
cards.a: **Liveness**: is the app stuck? If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. **Readiness**: can it take traffic? If it fails, the pod is taken out of the Service, but not restarted.

cards.q: What is a Kubernetes startup probe for?
cards.a: Apps that start slowly. The other probes wait until the startup probe passes.

cards.q: How do services find each other in Kubernetes?
cards.a: You create a **Service**, like `payment`. Other pods just call `payment`, and Kubernetes forwards each call to a healthy pod. Teams on Kubernetes often need no separate registry.

cards.q: What is an API gateway?
cards.a: One front door for all your backend services. Every request from outside comes to it first. It checks the request, then sends it to the right service.

cards.q: What are the main jobs of an API gateway?
cards.a: Routing, login checks (authentication), rate limiting, TLS termination, changing requests, combining answers, caching, logging and metrics, and versioning.

cards.q: In what order does an API gateway check each request?
cards.a: Valid login token? If not, `401 Unauthorized`. Under the rate limit? If not, `429 Too Many Requests`. Then it finds the service by path and forwards the request.

cards.q: How does an API gateway route requests to services?
cards.a: It keeps rules like "`/orders/**` goes to order-service". It finds each service's current addresses through service discovery and spreads requests across them like a load balancer.

cards.q: Why check login tokens at the gateway instead of in each service?
cards.a: Otherwise every service writes the same check, maybe in different languages, and it is easy to get one wrong. With a gateway, the check happens once, at the door.

cards.q: Why must the gateway remove any `X-User-Id` header the client sent?
cards.a: Services trust that header for the user's ID, because only the gateway can reach them. If the client's copy stayed, anyone could send `X-User-Id: 1` and act as another user.

cards.q: Which check stays in the service, even with an API gateway?
cards.a: **Authorization**: "may user 42 cancel order 7?" Only the order service knows who owns order 7. The gateway only checks who you are (authentication).

cards.q: What is the difference between an API gateway and a load balancer?
cards.a: A **load balancer** spreads traffic across copies of the same service. A **gateway** sends requests to different services and applies API rules. A load balancer manages traffic; a gateway manages APIs.

cards.q: What are the downsides of an API gateway?
cards.a: One more hop (a few ms), a single point of failure if you run only one copy, a possible bottleneck since all traffic goes through it, and too much logic if business rules creep in.

cards.q: How should you run an API gateway safely?
cards.a: Run several copies behind a load balancer, so it is not a single point of failure. Keep it to routing and shared checks, or it becomes a small monolith that every team must change.

cards.q: What is a backend for frontend (BFF)?
cards.a: A separate gateway for each kind of client, such as one for the mobile app and one for the website. Each one shapes the answers for its own client.

cards.q: When should you add an API gateway to a design?
cards.a: When there are several services, or a public API with keys and limits. With a single service, a load balancer is enough.

cards.q: What are some ready-made API gateways?
cards.a: Amazon API Gateway (run for you by AWS), Kong (open source, built on top of Nginx) and Apigee (from Google). Netflix built its own, called Zuul.

cards.q: What is a monolith?
cards.a: One app that does everything. All the code lives in one codebase, and it is built and deployed together, as one unit. It can still scale by running many copies behind a load balancer.

cards.q: What are microservices?
cards.a: Many small services. Each one does one job, runs on its own and is deployed on its own. They talk to each other over the network.

cards.q: What are the good sides of a monolith?
cards.a: Simple to build, test and deploy. Fast function calls with no network. Easy transactions, since there is one database. Easy to debug: one log, one place to look.

cards.q: What goes wrong with a monolith as it grows?
cards.a: Every change means deploying the whole app, teams get in each other's way, one bug can take everything down, you must scale everything together, and you are stuck with one tech stack.

cards.q: What are the good sides of microservices?
cards.a: Teams deploy on their own, you scale only what is busy, failures stay small if designed well, and each service can use the right tool for its job.

cards.q: What are the downsides of microservices?
cards.a: Network calls are slower and can fail, there are no simple transactions across services (you need patterns like Saga), debugging needs tracing, and there is much more to run.

cards.q: What does it mean that each microservice owns its own data?
cards.a: No other service reads its database directly. Services talk to each other through APIs or messages.

cards.q: What are three-tier architecture and SOA?
cards.a: **Three-tier** splits an app by technical layer: presentation, application (business logic) and data. **SOA** splits a system into a few large, often shared services that talk through a central bus (ESB).

cards.q: How are microservices different from SOA?
cards.a: They are like a lighter SOA: smaller services, each owned by one team, each with its own data, talking through simple pipes (plain HTTP or a simple queue) instead of a smart central bus.

cards.q: When should you pick a monolith?
cards.a: When the product is new and still changing, the team is small, you don't yet know the clean lines between parts, and building fast matters most.

cards.q: When should you pick microservices?
cards.a: When many teams need to ship on their own, parts have very different load or need different tech, and you already have good automation: deploys, monitoring, tracing.

cards.q: What is a modular monolith?
cards.a: One app with one deploy, but the code is split into clear modules with strict rules about who may call whom. You can still pull a module out into its own service later.

cards.q: What is Conway's Law, and what does it mean for microservices?
cards.a: A system's design ends up looking like the way the company's teams talk to each other. Microservices mostly solve a people problem, so split services along team lines.

cards.q: How should you move from a monolith to microservices?
cards.a: Piece by piece with the **strangler pattern**, never a big rewrite: put a gateway in front, move one part with clear edges to a new service with its own data, send its traffic there, repeat.

cards.q: Why did Amazon Prime Video merge one tool back into a monolith?
cards.a: Its video-quality tool was built from many small serverless pieces, and passing data between them was expensive and hit scaling limits. As one app, its cost dropped by over 90%.

cards.q: What is capacity estimation?
cards.a: Quick, rough math (back-of-the-envelope math) that tells you how big a system must be: how many requests per second, how much storage, how much network traffic.

cards.q: How exact does capacity estimation need to be?
cards.a: Only the **order of magnitude**: is it 100, 10,000 or 1 million requests per second? Being off by 10% doesn't matter. Being off by 10 times does.

cards.q: What are the handy shortcuts for multiplying counts by sizes?
cards.a: A million × 1 KB = 1 GB. A billion × 1 KB = 1 TB. A million × 1 MB = 1 TB.

cards.q: What are the rough sizes of a character, an int, a long, a timestamp and a UUID?
cards.a: An English character: 1 byte. An int: 4 bytes. A long: 8 bytes. A timestamp: 8 bytes. A UUID: 16 bytes (36 as text).

cards.q: Roughly how big are a chat message, a user profile row, a photo and a minute of HD video?
cards.a: A chat message with IDs and time: a few hundred bytes. A profile row: about 1 KB. A compressed photo: about 200 KB to 2 MB. 1 minute of HD video: about 50 to 100 MB.

cards.q: How many seconds are in a day, and what do you round it to?
cards.a: 86,400. Round it to **100,000** (10⁵) for easy math. A month is about 2.5 million seconds, and a year about 30 million.

cards.q: How do you turn requests per day into requests per second?
cards.a: Divide by 100,000. 1 million a day ≈ 10 per second, 100 million ≈ 1,000, 1 billion ≈ 10,000. (1 million a day is about 12 per second exactly, but that is close enough.)

cards.q: How long do a memory read, an SSD random read and a round trip inside one data center take?
cards.a: Memory (RAM): 100 ns. Random read from an SSD: 100 µs (0.1 ms). Round trip inside one data center: 0.5 ms.

cards.q: How long do reading 1 MB from an SSD, an indexed query and an HDD seek take?
cards.a: Reading 1 MB in a row from an SSD: 1 ms. A simple database query using an index: 1 to 10 ms. A hard disk (HDD) seek: 10 ms.

cards.q: How long is a network round trip across an ocean, and what does that teach you?
cards.a: USA East Coast ↔ Europe: about 80 ms. India ↔ USA: about 200 ms. Across an ocean is expensive, so put data near users and avoid many round trips.

cards.q: Roughly how many requests per second can one app server and one SQL database handle?
cards.a: App server: 1,000 to 10,000 simple API calls. SQL database: about 10,000 to 50,000 simple reads using an index, on a well-sized server; fewer for writes and heavy queries. Say out loud that these are rough guesses.

cards.q: Roughly how much can one Redis server and one Kafka broker handle?
cards.a: Redis: about 100,000 operations per second. A Kafka broker: hundreds of thousands of messages per second.

cards.q: What are rough one-machine limits for connections, RAM, SSD and network?
cards.a: Open WebSocket connections: hundreds of thousands on a well-tuned server. RAM: 64 to 512 GB is common. SSD: a few TB to tens of TB. Network: 10 Gbps or more (10 Gbps ≈ 1 GB per second); big cloud machines get 25 to 100 Gbps or more.

cards.q: How do you get average and peak QPS from daily active users (DAU)?
cards.a: Requests per day = DAU × actions per user per day. Average QPS = requests per day ÷ 100,000. Peak QPS ≈ average × 2 or 3 (more for very spiky apps, like ticket sales).

cards.q: Why estimate reads and writes separately?
cards.a: They scale in different ways. One app may need read scaling (like a photo app), while another needs write scaling (like a chat app).

cards.q: How do you estimate storage per year?
cards.a: Storage per day = new items per day × size of one item. Per year = × 365 (or 400 for easy math). Databases usually keep 3 copies, so the real disk needed is about 3 times more.

cards.q: Where do big files like photos and videos go in your design?
cards.a: Keep them apart from small data. Big files go to object storage like Amazon S3, and only their links go in the database.

cards.q: Photo app: 10 million daily users each view 50 photos. What read QPS, and what decision follows?
cards.a: 500 million views a day ÷ 100,000 = 5,000 per second, about 15,000 at peak. One database might manage it, but it would run too busy, and busy servers get slow. We want headroom, so add a cache and read replicas.

cards.q: Photo app: 1 million new photos a day. What write QPS, and is sharding needed?
cards.a: 1 million ÷ 100,000 = 10 writes per second, about 30 at peak. One primary database handles this easily, so no sharding is needed.

cards.q: Photo app: 1 million new 500 KB photos a day. How much storage, and where does it go?
cards.a: 1 million × 500 KB = 500 GB a day, about 180 TB a year. The photos go to object storage (S3), not the database.

cards.q: How do you estimate bandwidth, and what does 5,000 photo views a second need?
cards.a: Bandwidth = QPS × the size of each response. 5,000 × 500 KB = 2.5 GB per second, more at peak. So serve photos from a CDN, not from app servers.

cards.q: Chat app: 50 million daily users send 40 messages each. What write QPS, and what follows?
cards.a: 2 billion a day ÷ 100,000 ≈ 20,000 per second, about 60,000 at peak. Far too many for one SQL primary: shard by chat ID, or use a write-friendly database like Cassandra.

cards.q: What should every capacity number lead to?
cards.a: A design decision: cache, shard, S3 or CDN. Ask: Does the data fit on one machine? Can one database take the writes? Is it read-heavy? Is the bandwidth huge?

cards.q: When should you keep capacity math short, or skip it?
cards.a: When the numbers clearly fit on one machine, when the interviewer says they don't need it, or when time is short. Then say "I'll assume it's big enough to need X" and move on.

cards.q: What are the tips for doing capacity math in an interview?
cards.a: Round hard (86,400 becomes 100,000), write your assumptions down, keep the units next to every number, and spend 2 to 3 minutes on it, not 10.

cards.q: Why did "Gangnam Style" nearly break YouTube's view counter?
cards.a: View counts were stored as a 32-bit number, which only goes up to about 2.1 billion. In December 2014 the video got close, and YouTube moved to a 64-bit number.

cards.q: Chat app: 2 billion messages a day, about 200 bytes each. How much storage per year, and what follows?
cards.a: 2 billion × 200 bytes = 400 GB a day. × 365 ≈ **150 TB a year**. That can't fit on one machine, so the data must be split across machines.

cards.q: Why do reads usually become the first database problem?
cards.a: Most apps are **read-heavy**: reads can be 100 times more than writes, or more. One database machine can only answer so many reads per second.

cards.q: In what order should you try fixes for a read-heavy system?
cards.a: Index → cache → read replicas → CDN → precompute. Try them in order; don't jump to the hard ones first.

cards.q: How does an index help reads?
cards.a: Like the index at the back of a book, it lets the database find a row without reading every row. Add it to the columns you search by.

cards.q: What is a read replica, and what is its catch?
cards.a: A copy of the database that only answers reads. The **primary** takes all writes and copies them over. Catch: a replica can be a little behind, so read a user's own new writes from the primary.

cards.q: What is precomputing?
cards.a: Preparing answers early. Instead of counting likes every time someone views a post, store the like count and update it when a like happens.

cards.q: Why should you say the read-to-write ratio early in an interview?
cards.a: It tells you the read-scaling pattern is needed. For example, "about 100 reads for every write" leads to a cache, read replicas and a CDN.

cards.q: How does Facebook keep reads off its MySQL databases?
cards.a: It puts a huge layer of Memcached cache servers in front of them. People read far more content than they create, so the cache answers most reads and the databases see only a small share.

cards.q: Why don't read replicas help with writes?
cards.a: Every copy must store every write. With one primary, all writes go through it, and each replica must copy every write, which adds work. Only splitting the data across machines adds write capacity.

cards.q: What should you do first, before bigger changes, to scale writes?
cards.a: Make each write cheaper. Every index is updated on every write, so remove indexes you don't use, and don't write data that hasn't changed.

cards.q: Why is batching writes faster than writing rows one by one?
cards.a: Every write has a fixed cost: a network round trip, starting a transaction, and saving to disk. Writing 1,000 rows in one go is much cheaper than 1,000 separate writes.

cards.q: What is buffering writes, and what does it cost?
cards.a: Keep writes in memory briefly, then save them together, like one "+1,250 views" per video every 5 seconds. A crash loses the buffered writes, so it suits view counts, not payments.

cards.q: How does a queue help with write spikes?
cards.a: The app puts each write in a queue and answers "got it" right away. Workers write at a steady speed the database can handle. If the database is down for a minute, the writes wait in the queue.

cards.q: What are the limits of using a queue for writes?
cards.a: The write isn't done right away, so the user may not see their change for a moment. And a queue only smooths spikes: if writes outpace the workers all day long, the queue just keeps growing.

cards.q: How does sharding scale writes?
cards.a: It splits the data across several databases, each with its own primary taking only its share of the writes: 10 shards take about 10 times the writes. Pick a shard key that spreads writes evenly.

cards.q: Which kinds of databases suit huge write volumes, metrics and very fast counters?
cards.a: Wide-column, LSM-based databases like Cassandra or ScyllaDB for messages, events and sensor data. Time-series databases like InfluxDB for metrics. Redis for very fast counters and short-lived data.

cards.q: What is the price of a write-friendly database like Cassandra?
cards.a: Fewer features: limited joins and transactions, and you must design your tables around your queries up front. In return, it shards for you as you add machines.

cards.q: Why is `UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1` a problem for a viral post?
cards.a: Thousands of likes per second all update the same row. The database locks the row for each update, so they all wait in one line. This is a **hot row**.

cards.q: How can you count likes at scale?
cards.a: Count in Redis with `INCR` and have a job save the totals every few seconds, batch increments in each app server, use sharded counters, use a HyperLogLog for unique counts, or send events to Kafka for a counting job.

cards.q: What is a sharded counter?
cards.a: One counter split into, say, 10 smaller counters. Each like adds 1 to a random one, and you add them all up to read the total. Now 10 writes can happen at the same time. Create the 10 rows up front, or the `UPDATE` finds no row and does nothing.

cards.q: Why does Google Firestore tell developers to shard counters?
cards.a: As of 2026, Firestore's docs warn that one document can't be updated at an unlimited rate (older docs said about once per second). For counters that change faster, they say to split the count across several documents and add them up when reading.
